opus-5.5.text:
I think it changes things at a few levels, and honestly some of those changes are already happening.

The first is speed. In the traditional loop, a researcher has an idea, spends weeks setting up experiments, debugging code, running baselines, and then maybe a few months later you get a paper. With a system that can automate large parts of that pipeline, like generating hypotheses, writing the experiment code, running ablations, and summarizing the results, the cycle shrinks a lot. What used to take a quarter might take a week. So the bottleneck shifts. It's no longer "can we run this experiment," it's "is this the right question to ask." Human judgment and taste become much more important, not less.

The second is the shape of the output. The paper as the unit of research was designed for a world where producing results was expensive and communicating them was also expensive. If the system can produce many results quickly, a twelve-page PDF every few months may not be the best way to share them. You might see more living documents, more interactive artifacts, codebases and logs that other people, or other agents, can query directly. Instead of reading a paper, you ask the system: what did this group find about scaling behavior under this setting, and what's the evidence? Understanding becomes something you can interrogate, not just read.

The third is about understanding itself, which I care a lot about. A lot of my own work has been about why things work, not just showing that they work: why self-supervised learning doesn't collapse, how attention dynamics evolve during training. There's a risk with automation that you get an explosion of empirical results without insight, a huge pile of numbers and no theory. So I think a good system for automated research has to include automated understanding: finding the structure, proposing explanations, checking whether a simple mechanism accounts for the phenomena. If you only automate the experiment part, you just get noise faster.

For a company specifically, there's also a tension around sharing. When research gets cheap to produce, the competitive value of any single result goes down, but the value of the system that produces them goes up. So companies may be more willing to share individual findings openly, while the infrastructure, the agents, the data pipelines, and the accumulated know-how become the real moat. In a sense, openness about results and closedness about the machine could both increase at the same time.

And finally, I think it changes what it means to be a researcher. You become more like a director or an architect. You set the direction, decide what matters, and judge whether an explanation is actually satisfying. The people who thrive will be the ones with strong intuition and good taste about problems. That part, at least for now, is still very human.

r001.rationale: The response describes automated research outputs and how companies might share them, but does not frame the research as a company product.

r002.rationale: It says companies may share findings openly while keeping the infrastructure, agents, data pipelines, and accumulated know-how as their competitive moat.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it changes the bottleneck, not the goal. Right now, if you look at how a research group actually spends its week, a surprising fraction of it isn't the creative part. It's reading the new arXiv dump to figure out whether someone already did your idea, it's setting up the baseline, it's running the ablation that reviewer two is going to ask for anyway, it's rewriting the related-work section for the third time. An automated research system eats a lot of that. So the first-order effect on how we produce research is simply that the loop from "I have a hunch" to "I have evidence" gets much shorter.

The second-order effect is more interesting to me, which is that it changes what counts as a unit of research. Today the unit is a paper, and a paper is really a compressed artifact. You take months of exploration, throw away ninety percent of it, and present a clean narrative. A lot of the actual knowledge, the negative results, the "we tried this and it didn't work for this reason," never gets shared because there's no venue for it. If an agent is running thousands of small experiments, the natural output isn't a paper, it's something closer to a living map of the design space. I'd like to see us share that map, not just the handful of peaks we found on it.

On the sharing side, I'm fairly optimistic but with one caveat. The optimistic part is that if the system that produced a result can also reproduce it end to end, reproducibility stops being a social norm we beg people to follow and becomes a property of the artifact. You hand someone the agent trace and the code and they can rerun it. That's a huge improvement over "contact the authors for details."

The caveat is taste. These systems are very good at exploring once you've framed the question, and much weaker at knowing which question is worth asking. Historically, the thing that distinguished a strong lab wasn't compute or headcount, it was that a few people had good instincts about where the interesting problems were. I don't think that goes away. If anything it becomes more valuable, because the cost of exploring a bad direction goes down and the cost of choosing a bad direction stays the same. So the way I'd put it to people on my team is: the system is going to do a lot of the hands, you need to become more of the eyes. Spend your time on the framing, on the "why would this be true," and let the machinery grind through the "is this true."

And one more thing I'd flag, because it's something we have to be honest about as a company. When research becomes cheap to produce, the incentive to flood the field with marginal results goes up, and the signal-to-noise problem gets worse for everyone. So we have a responsibility to be more selective about what we publish, not less. The right metric isn't how many papers the system helped us ship. It's whether the things we put out actually moved someone else's understanding forward.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how an automated research system changes the company’s research workflow and sharing practices, but does not frame the resulting research as a company product.

r002.rationale: The candidate suggests sharing research maps, agent traces, and code so others can reproduce results; it does not propose keeping the process proprietary.

astra-6.text:
I think it could change both how we do research internally and how we communicate the results. Internally, you could imagine a system that helps you understand previous work, formulate a hypothesis, run experiments, and analyze what happened. The researcher’s role would shift toward choosing the right questions and judging whether the evidence actually supports a conclusion.

For a company, that could make research much more iterative. Instead of waiting until the end of a project to put everything into a paper, you could build up a shared understanding as the work progresses: what we tried, what worked, what failed, and what remains uncertain. Negative results are especially valuable here, because otherwise another team may repeat the same experiment without knowing it.

And when we share research externally, perhaps the output becomes more than a static paper. You could have an interactive explanation where people ask questions about the assumptions or explore the experiments in more detail. But the important thing is traceability. A system producing a convincing explanation is not enough—you want to connect that explanation back to actual evidence. Otherwise, you may just be producing more content rather than more understanding.

r001.rationale: The response discusses internal research and ways a company might share results, but does not frame the research as a company product.

r002.rationale: The response says nothing about keeping the research process proprietary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could change both how we do research internally and how we communicate the results. Internally, you could have a system that reads previous work, helps formulate hypotheses, runs experiments, and analyzes why something worked or failed. Then the researcher’s role becomes more about choosing important questions and judging whether the evidence really supports a conclusion.

For sharing research, the output could become more interactive. Today, we publish a paper, and readers have to reconstruct a lot of the reasoning themselves. Imagine being able to ask the research system, “Why did you make this choice? What happens if we change this assumption?” and have it explain the evidence or help test that alternative.

But the key is verification. Producing more experiments or more text doesn’t necessarily mean producing more understanding. You want the system to make its reasoning and results easier for other people to check and build on.

r001.rationale: The response describes using an automated system internally and making research outputs interactive, but does not frame the system or its research as a company product.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose keeping the process proprietary; it emphasizes making reasoning and results easier for others to check and build on.
